claims.claim: Meiotic drive loci can be transmitted to up to 100% of gametes instead of the expected 50%.
claims.source: Rather than being transmitted to 50% of the progeny of a heterozygote, these selfish loci use a variety of tactics to promote their own transmission into up to 100% of the gametes (Sandler and Novitski, 1957; Zimmering et al., 1970).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Sandler and Novitski, 1957; Zimmering et al., 1970).

claims.claim: Different natural S. pombe isolates contain between 4 and 14 predicted wtf drivers.
claims.source: Different natural isolates contain between 4 and 14 predicted wtf drivers, almost all of which are found on chromosome 3 (Bowen et al., 2003; Eickbush et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Bowen et al., 2003; Eickbush et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Almost all wtf drivers are found on chromosome 3.
claims.source: Different natural isolates contain between 4 and 14 predicted wtf drivers, almost all of which are found on chromosome 3 (Bowen et al., 2003; Eickbush et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Bowen et al., 2003; Eickbush et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Each wtf meiotic driver encodes two proteins from two largely overlapping transcripts with distinct start sites: a poison (Wtfpoison) and an antidote (Wtfantidote).
claims.source: Each wtf meiotic driver encodes two proteins from two largely overlapping transcripts with distinct start sites: a poison (Wtfpoison) and an antidote (Wtfantidote) (Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017).

claims.claim: In wtf+/wtf- heterozygotes, all developing spores are exposed to Wtfpoison, but only those inheriting wtf+ express the corresponding Wtfantidote.
claims.source: In wtf+/wtf- heterozygotes, all the developing meiotic products (spores) are exposed to the Wtfpoison, but only those that inherit the wtf+ allele express the corresponding Wtfantidote and neutralize the poison.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017).

claims.claim: The poison and antidote proteins of a given wtf meiotic driver share more than 200 amino acid residues.
claims.source: The poison and antidote proteins of a given wtf meiotic driver share a considerable length of amino acid sequence (>200 residues) (Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017).

claims.claim: A mismatch of two amino acids within the C-terminus can disrupt the ability of a Wtfantidote to neutralize a Wtfpoison.
claims.source: Strikingly, even a mismatch of two amino acids within the C-terminus can disrupt the ability of a Wtfantidote to neutralize a Wtfpoison (Bravo Núñez et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation (Bravo Núñez et al., 2018).

claims.claim: The antidote of a given wtf gene generally does not neutralize poisons produced by other wtf drivers with distinct sequences.
claims.source: The antidote of a given wtf gene generally does not neutralize poisons produced by other wtf drivers with distinct sequences (Bravo Núñez et al., 2018; Bravo Núñez et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Bravo Núñez et al., 2018; Bravo Núñez et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Heterozygous, competing wtf drivers provide a selective advantage to atypical spores that inherit more than a haploid complement of wtf drivers.
claims.source: Here, we find that heterozygous, competing wtf drivers provide a selective advantage to atypical spores that inherit more than a haploid complement of wtf drivers.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: The selective advantage of atypical spores is due to the preferential elimination of haploid spores.
claims.source: This selective advantage is due to the preferential elimination of haploid spores, as these spores are killed by the wtf driver(s) they do not inherit.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: The selected atypical spores include aneuploids, diploids, and spores inheriting wtf gene duplications resulting from unequal crossovers.
claims.source: The selected atypical spores include aneuploids, diploids, and spores inheriting wtf gene duplications resulting from unequal crossovers between homologous chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Competing wtf drivers generate an environment where variants that disrupt meiotic chromosome segregation can increase fitness.
claims.source: We use a combination of empirical analyses and modeling to demonstrate that competing wtf drivers generate an environment where variants that disrupt meiotic chromosome segregation can increase fitness.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data and modeling.

claims.claim: S. pombe cells generally exist as haploids but will mate to form diploids when starved of nutrients.
claims.source: S. pombe cells generally exist as haploids but will mate to form diploids when starved of nutrients.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation (Egel, 2004; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: When starvation signal is continued, S. pombe diploids will proceed into meiosis resulting in the production of spores.
claims.source: If this starvation signal is continued, these diploids will proceed into meiosis resulting in the production of spores (Egel, 2004; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation (Egel, 2004; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: All known S. pombe isolates share an average DNA sequence identity of >99% for nonrepetitive regions.
claims.source: All known S. pombe isolates share an average DNA sequence identity of >99% for nonrepetitive regions, and nearly all of these isolates contain three chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about S. pombe isolates.

claims.claim: Nearly all S. pombe isolates contain three chromosomes.
claims.source: All known S. pombe isolates share an average DNA sequence identity of >99% for nonrepetitive regions, and nearly all of these isolates contain three chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about S. pombe isolates.

claims.claim: Outcrossing S. pombe often yields diploids that exhibit low fertility.
claims.source: Despite minimal sequence divergence between the strains, outcrossing often yields diploids that exhibit low fertility (i.e. they produce few viable spores) (Avelar et al., 2013; Gutz and Doe, 1975; Hu et al., 2017; Jeffares et al., 2015; Singh and Klar, 2002; Zanders et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Avelar et al., 2013; Gutz and Doe, 1975; Hu et al., 2017; Jeffares et al., 2015; Singh and Klar, 2002; Zanders et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Differences in karyotype between isolates and pervasive meiotic drive are the two demonstrated causes of infertility in heterozygous S. pombe diploids.
claims.source: Differences in karyotype (such as chromosomal rearrangements) between isolates and pervasive meiotic drive are the two demonstrated causes of infertility in heterozygous S. pombe diploids (Avelar et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017; Zanders et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations (Avelar et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017; Zanders et al., 2014).

claims.claim: The majority of surviving spores from Sp/Sk heterozygotes are heterozygous aneuploids or diploids containing both the Sp copy and Sk copy of chromosome 3.
claims.source: Although these Sp/Sk heterozygotes make few viable spores, the majority of the surviving spores are heterozygous aneuploids or diploids, as they contain both the Sp copy and Sk copy of chromosome 3 (Zanders et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation (Zanders et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Disomy of chromosome 3 is the only tolerable aneuploidy within Sp.
claims.source: Disomy of chromosome 3 is the only tolerable aneuploidy within Sp, as spores disomic for chromosomes 1 or 2, or spores lacking any of the three chromosomes are inviable (Niwa et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation (Niwa et al., 2006).

claims.claim: Diploid spores possessing an extra copy of every chromosome are viable.
claims.source: Additionally, diploid spores, or spores possessing an extra copy of every chromosome are viable.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claims.claim: The disomic state of chromosome 3 aneuploids is unstable and the extra chromosome 3 is quickly shed as the spores grow and form colonies.
claims.source: Furthermore, the disomic state of chromosome 3 aneuploids is unstable and the extra chromosome 3 is quickly shed as the spores grow and form colonies (Niwa et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation (Niwa et al., 2006).

claims.claim: Each of the novel heterozygous diploids tested had low viable spore yields compared to homozygous diploid controls.
claims.source: Similar to the previously characterized Sp/Sk heterozygotes, our genetic analyses revealed that each of the novel heterozygous diploids we tested had low viable spore yields compared to homozygous diploid controls (Figure 1B, compare diploids 2–7 to diploids 8–12).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The reduced viable spore yields in heterozygotes are likely due to increased spore death.
claims.source: These reduced yields are likely due to increased spore death in the heterozygotes (Hu et al., 2017; Jeffares et al., 2015; Singh and Klar, 2002; Zanders et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on data and supported by citations (Hu et al., 2017; Jeffares et al., 2015; Singh and Klar, 2002; Zanders et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Heterozygous diploids frequently produced spores that grew into small colonies with irregular shapes, a hallmark of aneuploidy.
claims.source: In addition to having low viable spore yields, the heterozygous diploids frequently produced spores that grew into small colonies with irregular shapes, a hallmark of aneuploidy (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Niwa et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, with citation (Niwa et al., 2006).

claims.claim: 34–78% of the viable spores produced by heterozygotes were determined to be disomic for chromosome 3.
claims.source: Consistent with this, 34–78% of the viable spores produced by heterozygotes were determined to be disomic for chromosome 3 as they inherited both centromere 3-linked markers (ade6+ and ade6Δ::hphMX6; Figure 1B, diploids 2–7).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The frequency of disomic spores was generally higher in heterozygotes than homozygotes.
claims.source: The frequency of disomic spores was generally higher in heterozygotes than homozygotes.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: There was considerable variation amongst the homozygotes with spore disomy frequencies ranging from 5–46%.
claims.source: However, there was considerable variation amongst the homozygotes with spore disomy frequencies ranging from 5–46% (Figure 1B, diploids 8–12).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: In diploids heterozygous for different wtf driving alleles, haploid spores will generally inherit either every Sp driver or every Sk driver.
claims.source: As a result, in diploids heterozygous for different wtf driving alleles, the drivers can be described as 'competing' as they exist on separate haplotypes and produce distinct Wtf proteins.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of wtf drivers.

claims.claim: Heterozygous disomic spores are more likely to inherit all the competing wtf drive alleles.
claims.source: However, heterozygous disomic spores are more likely to inherit all the competing wtf drive alleles.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of wtf drivers and chromosome inheritance.

claims.claim: Disomic spores that inherit every wtf driver should survive, as they will contain every Wtfantidote necessary to counteract the Wtf poisons.
claims.source: These disomic spores should thus survive, as they will contain every Wtfantidote necessary to counteract the Wtf poisons (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of wtf drivers, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Sp/Sk heterozygotes do not make more disomic spores per meiosis than Sp or Sk homozygotes.
claims.source: Consistent with this model, Sp/Sk heterozygotes do not make more disomic spores per meiosis than Sp or Sk homozygotes (Zanders et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation (Zanders et al., 2014).

claims.claim: 63% of the viable spores generated by the double driver heterozygote appeared to be disomic.
claims.source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we found that 63% of the viable spores generated by the double driver heterozygote appeared to be disomic as they inherited both alleles at ade6 (ade6-:FY29033 wtf36:natMX4 and ade6-:Sp wtf13:hphMX6).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The control diploid (no heterozygous wtf drivers) generated 4% disomic viable spores.
claims.source: This was considerably higher than the control diploid (no heterozygous wtf drivers) in which 4% of the viable spores displayed this phenotype (Figure 2C, compare diploid 13 to 14).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Many of the viable spores produced by the double driver heterozygote generated small, misshapen colonies characteristic of aneuploids.
claims.source: Additionally, many of the viable spores produced by the double driver heterozygote generated small, misshapen colonies characteristic of aneuploids.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by observations.

claims.claim: The fertility of the double driver heterozygote was 20-fold lower than the control diploid.
claims.source: Finally, the fertility of the double driver heterozygote was 20-fold lower than the control diploid (Figure 2C, compare diploid 13 to diploid 14).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Sk wtf28poison/Sk wtf4poison heterozygotes had very low viable spore yields, but did not exhibit a higher frequency of disomic spores than control diploids.
claims.source: We found that Sk wtf28poison/Sk wtf4poison heterozygotes had very low viable spore yields, but did not exhibit a higher frequency of disomic spores than control diploids (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The number of disomic spores produced per cell placed on sporulation media did not increase between the double driver heterozygote and the control diploid.
claims.source: We found that the number of disomic spores produced per cell placed on sporulation media did not increase between the double driver heterozygote and the control diploid (Figure 2—figure supplement 4, compare diploid 13 to diploid 14).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Disomic spores generated from diploids carrying multiple sets of heterozygous wtf meiotic drivers are enriched in the surviving population due to the destruction of haploid spores, rather than due to Wtf proteins increasing the rate of meiotic chromosome missegregation.
claims.source: Together, our results are consistent with our hypothesis that disomic spores generated from diploids carrying multiple sets of heterozygous wtf meiotic drivers are enriched in the surviving population due to the destruction of haploid spores, rather than due to Wtf proteins increasing the rate of meiotic chromosome missegregation.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claims.claim: The Sp/Sk mosaic diploid is heterozygous for eight known or predicted wtf meiotic drivers.
claims.source: For these experiments, we started with an Sp/Sk mosaic diploid strain that is heterozygous for eight known or predicted wtf meiotic drivers (Bravo Núñez et al., 2020; Eickbush et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental strain with citations (Bravo Núñez et al., 2020; Eickbush et al., 2019).

claims.claim: The Sp/Sk mosaic diploid is homozygous for Sk chromosomes 1 and 2 but is heterozygous for most of chromosome 3 for Sp- and Sk-derived sequences.
claims.source: This mosaic diploid is homozygous for Sk chromosomes 1 and 2 but is heterozygous for most of chromosome 3 for Sp- and Sk-derived sequences (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental strain shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The viable spores generated by the rec12Δ Sp/Sk mosaic diploid were almost exclusively (94%) heterozygous disomes for chromosome 3.
claims.source: Consistent with our previous observations in a similar mosaic diploid (Nuckolls et al., 2017), we saw that the viable spores generated by this diploid were almost exclusively (94%) heterozygous disomes for chromosome 3 (Figure 3B, diploid 17).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3B with citation (Nuckolls et al., 2017).

claims.claim: rec12Δ Sk homozygous diploids generate only 27% disomic spores.
claims.source: Lack of recombination is, however, insufficient to explain the majority of the phenotype, as rec12Δ Sk homozygous diploids generate only 27% disomic spores (Figure 3B, diploid 19).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Deleting both Sp wtf13 and Sp wtf4 significantly decreased the frequency of chromosome 3 heterozygous disomes from 94% to 67% in the rec12Δ mosaic diploid.
claims.source: Consistent with our hypothesis, deleting both Sp drivers significantly decreased the frequency of chromosome 3 heterozygous disomes (from 94% to 67%; Figure 3B, diploids 17 and 18), although it did not significantly increase fertility.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Deleting only one of the two Sp drivers (Sp wtf13 or Sp wtf4) was sufficient to significantly decrease the frequency of disomic spores in the rec12Δ mosaic diploid.
claims.source: Deleting only one of the two Sp drivers was also sufficient to significantly decrease the frequency of disomic spores (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, diploids 47 and 48).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Deleting only one of the six predicted Sk drivers (wtf4) had no effect on disomy frequency in the rec12Δ mosaic diploid.
claims.source: However, deleting only one of the six predicted Sk drivers (wtf4) had no effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, diploid 49).

claims.claim: The rec12+/rec12Δ mosaic diploid had low fertility, similar to that of the rec12Δ Sp/Sk mosaic diploid.
claims.source: We observed that this rec12+/rec12Δ diploid had low fertility, similar to that of the rec12Δ Sp/Sk mosaic diploid (Figure 3B, compare diploid 17 to diploid 20).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: 68% of the viable spores generated by the rec12+/rec12Δ mosaic diploid appeared to be disomic for chromosome 3.
claims.source: We found that 68% of the viable spores generated by this mosaic appeared to be disomic for chromosome 3.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Deleting both Sp wtf4 and Sp wtf13 in the rec12+/rec12Δ mosaic diploid significantly increased fertility and decreased disomy at ade6 amongst the viable spores from 68% to 27%.
claims.source: Deleting both Sp wtf4 and Sp wtf13 in the rec12+/rec12Δ mosaic diploid significantly increased fertility and decreased disomy at ade6 amongst the viable spores from 68% to 27% (Figure 3B, diploids 20 and 21).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: In the Sk double driver heterozygote, the genetic distance between ade6 and ura4 decreased significantly from 75 cM to 44 cM compared to the Sk control.
claims.source: The ade6 and ura4 loci are over 75 cM apart in the Sk control (Figure 2—figure supplement 5). In the Sk double driver heterozygotes, this distance decreased significantly to 44 cM (p-value=0.03, G-test).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: In the mosaic diploids with all drivers intact, ade6 and ura4 were 43 cM apart.
claims.source: In the mosaic diploids with all drivers intact, we observed ade6 and ura4 were 43 cM apart (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), similar to the 62 cM previously observed in Sp/Sk hybrids (Zanders et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 with citation (Zanders et al., 2014).

claims.claim: When Sp wtf4 and Sp wtf13 were deleted from the mosaic strain, the observed genetic distance between ade6 and ura4 decreased significantly to 11 cM.
claims.source: However, when Sp wtf4 and Sp wtf13 were deleted from the mosaic strain, the observed genetic distance decreased significantly to 11 cM (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; p-value<0.01, G-test).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Meiotic drivers can directly affect recombination landscapes.
claims.source: Overall, our results demonstrate that meiotic drivers can directly affect recombination landscapes.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by the recombination frequency data.

claims.claim: Sk wtf4/Sk wtf28 heterozygous diploids had decreased fertility (13% of the control diploid).

claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: 77% of the viable spores from Sk wtf4/Sk wtf28 heterozygous diploids appeared to be disomic for chromosome 3.

claims.claim: An unequal interhomolog crossover event at the ade6 locus could lead to duplication of the wtf driver found on the opposite haplotype.
claims.source: We reasoned that an unequal interhomolog crossover event at the ade6 locus could have led to duplication of the wtf driver found on the opposite haplotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data, illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The unequal crossover events in Sk wtf4/Sk wtf28 heterozygote were Rec12-dependent.
claims.source: Consistent with the idea that a crossover placed the competing wtf drivers on one haplotype in the Sk wtf4/Sk wtf28 diploid meiosis, the events were Rec12-dependent (Figure 4, diploid 26).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 4.

claims.claim: A PCR product consistent with the recombination event was detected in 19 out of the 22 haploid G418R HygR spore colonies tested from Sk wtf4/Sk wtf28 heterozygote.
claims.source: In addition, we detected a PCR product consistent with the recombination event in 19 out of the 22 haploid G418R HygR spore colonies tested (Figure 4, diploid 24, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, and Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, and Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Deleting rec12 imposed no fitness cost on Sp/Sk heterozygotes compared to the Sp/Sp or Sk/Sk homozygotes.

claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation (Zanders et al., 2014) and supported by data in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Rec12 did not significantly promote fertility in CBS5680/Sp, JB844/Sp, CBS5680/Sk, and JB844/Sk heterozygotes as it did in homozygotes.

claims.claim: Deleting sgo1 and rec10 had a lower fitness cost in the background with heterozygous wtf drivers than in the background without wtf competition (~3 fold decrease compared to a 6–7-fold decrease).

claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Deleting moa1 or rec8 had no effect on fitness in diploids with heterozygous wtf drivers, despite the fact that these mutations decrease fertility by 4- and 6-fold, respectively, in the absence of wtf driver competition.

claims.claim: Deleting one copy of moa1 did not significantly alter the frequency of disomic spores in the absence of wtf driver competition.

claims.claim: Heterozygosity for moa1 did not suppress the fitness costs of wtf competition.

claims.claim: Deleting one copy of rec8 significantly increased the production of disomic spores in a background without heterozygous wtf drivers.

claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: rec8 exhibits haploinsufficiency and reducing Rec8 protein levels may lead to chromosome segregation errors during meiosis.
claims.source: This suggests that rec8 exhibits haploinsufficiency and reducing Rec8 protein levels may lead to chromosome segregation errors during meiosis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data.

claims.claim: rec8 heterozygosity increased the fertility of diploids with competing drivers.
claims.source: As hypothesized, rec8 heterozygosity also increased the fertility of diploids with competing drivers (Figure 6B, diploid 29).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The higher the strength of drive (t), the lower the number of drivers required for mutant invasion.
claims.source: Interestingly, the higher the strength of drive (t), the lower the number of drivers required for mutant invasion (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the population genetic modeling shown in Figure 7B.

claims.source: Importantly, our empirical work demonstrates that drive strength is generally high (t >0.9) and that there are ample distinct wtf driver haplotypes (Eickbush et al., 2019) leaving parameter space for mutants to invade even if they incur considerable costs (sm and ss) (Appendix 1—figure 1; Bravo Núñez et al., 2018; Bravo Núñez et al., 2020; Eickbush et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2017; Nuckolls et al., 2017).

claims.claim: There are ample distinct wtf driver haplotypes in S. pombe.

claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from empirical work with citation (Eickbush et al., 2019).

claims.claim: When S. pombe inbreeds to generate homozygotes, the effects of wtf meiotic drivers are largely invisible as every spore inherits the necessary Wtf antidotes required to neutralize the Wtf poisons.

results.result: Heterozygous diploids generated by outcrossing different S. pombe isolates exhibit low viable spore yields and produce high frequencies (34-78%) of disomic spores for chromosome 3, with considerable variation among homozygous isolates (5-46% disomy).
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C37 provide converging evidence from multiple heterozygous crosses showing consistent patterns of reduced fertility and elevated disomy. The data include quantitative measurements across multiple isolates with appropriate controls (homozygous diploids), and the findings are consistent with prior work (C28). The variation observed among homozygotes (C37) is well-documented with Figure 1 data.

results.result: In diploids with two sets of competing wtf drivers, 63% of viable spores are disomic compared to 4% in controls, with 20-fold reduced fertility. This enrichment results from selective death of haploid spores rather than increased production of disomic spores per meiosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C48 provide strong experimental evidence using engineered strains with defined wtf driver configurations. The key control experiments (C46-C47) rule out alternative mechanisms by showing that poison-only alleles don't increase disomy and that disomic spore production per meiosis is unchanged. The convergence of multiple lines of evidence supports the proposed mechanism.

results.result: In Sp/Sk mosaic diploids heterozygous for eight wtf drivers, deleting the two Sp drivers significantly reduces disomy frequency from 94% to 67% (rec12Δ background) or from 68% to 27% (rec12+/rec12Δ background), demonstrating that wtf driver competition contributes to high disomy.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C58 present systematic genetic dissection experiments with appropriate controls. The deletion experiments show dose-dependent effects (single vs. double deletions, C54-C55) and work in both recombination-deficient and recombination-proficient backgrounds. However, the incomplete rescue (C53, C58) indicates wtf competition alone doesn't fully explain the phenotype, which the authors acknowledge.

results.result: Meiotic drivers directly affect recombination landscapes: genetic distance between ade6 and ura4 decreased from 75 cM to 44 cM in double driver heterozygotes, and from 43 cM to 11 cM when Sp drivers were deleted from mosaic diploids.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 provide quantitative recombination frequency measurements with statistical significance (p<0.05). The bidirectional effects (both increases and decreases in apparent recombination) depending on driver configuration support the conclusion. The measurements use appropriate genetic markers and sufficient sample sizes (>100 spores analyzed per cross based on figures).

results.result: In diploids with competing wtf drivers at a single locus (Sk wtf4/Sk wtf28), 77% of viable spores inherit both drivers, but surprisingly 84.6% of these are haploid rather than aneuploid/diploid. PCR analysis detected unequal crossover products in 19/22 tested colonies, indicating wtf gene duplication via recombination.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C69 present an unexpected finding with thorough characterization. Multiple independent assays (colony morphology, marker maintenance, phloxin B staining, microscopy, PCR) converge to identify the ploidy of survivors (Figure 4). The Rec12-dependence (C68) and PCR detection (C69) provide strong mechanistic support. This represents a distinct survival mechanism from the disomy observed in other experiments.

results.result: Deleting rec12 imposes no fitness cost in outcrossed S. pombe heterozygotes with multiple competing wtf drivers, contrasting with the 3-fold fertility decrease observed in homozygotes or diploids with only one set of competing drivers.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73 demonstrate context-dependent fitness effects with appropriate controls across multiple strain backgrounds. The dose-dependence (one vs. two sets of competing drivers, C72-C73) strengthens the conclusion. The data are consistent with the model that benefits of increased disomy can offset costs of disrupted recombination when multiple drivers compete.

results.result: Mutations disrupting meiotic chromosome segregation (rec10Δ, sgo1Δ, moa1Δ, rec8Δ) have reduced or eliminated fitness costs in the presence of competing wtf drivers. Notably, rec8 heterozygosity increases disomy in controls and increases fertility in driver competition backgrounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C80 present systematic analysis of multiple meiotic genes with consistent patterns. The rec8 haploinsufficiency finding (C78-C80) is particularly well-supported with both the phenotype (increased disomy without drivers) and the rescue (increased fertility with drivers). The graded effects across different mutations strengthen the overall conclusion about context-dependent fitness landscapes.

results.result: Population genetic modeling shows that higher drive strength (t) reduces the number of drivers required for invasion of segregation-infidelity mutants. Empirical data demonstrate drive strength is generally high (t>0.9) in S. pombe with ample distinct wtf driver haplotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 integrate mathematical modeling with empirical observations. The modeling provides theoretical framework (C82, Figure 7B) while empirical work (C83-C84) establishes that S. pombe parameters fall within the range where mutants can invade. The convergence of theory and observation supports the conclusion, though the model makes simplifying assumptions acknowledged in the text.

results.result: wtf drivers generate a fitness landscape where atypical spores (aneuploids, diploids, and spores with wtf duplications) gain selective advantage through preferential survival, and mutations disrupting meiotic fidelity can become beneficial by increasing production of such spores.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C18-C21, and C98-C99 represent the central thesis supported by multiple experimental results throughout the manuscript. The convergence of evidence from natural isolate surveys, engineered strains, genetic deletions, and population modeling provides strong support. This integrative result synthesizes findings from multiple experimental approaches.

results.result: S. pombe isolates show substantial natural variation in meiotic fidelity, with some generating up to 46% aneuploid/diploid spores, and even the most faithful strains produce ~5% disomic spores, suggesting chromosome 3 missegregates in ~10% of meioses.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C37, and C103 document natural variation with quantitative measurements across multiple isolates (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3). The inference about missegregation frequency (C103) is reasonable given that each meiosis produces 4 spores. This establishes important baseline variation in the system, though the evolutionary origins remain unclear.

results.result: The effects of wtf drivers on meiosis are indirect: Wtf proteins act after meiosis completion through spore killing, not by directly affecting recombination or chromosome segregation mechanisms, yet they create selective pressures that can favor altered meiotic outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 and C85-C88 establish the indirect nature of wtf effects through logical inference and lack of evidence for direct mechanisms. The timing of Wtf action (post-meiosis, C88) and the absence of evidence for direct participation in meiotic processes (C87) support this conclusion. This mechanistic insight is important for understanding how drivers shape meiotic evolution.

results.result: Background on meiotic drivers and wtf system: Killer meiotic drivers destroy gametes lacking the driver allele and can achieve up to 100% transmission. S. pombe contains 4-14 wtf drivers (mostly on chromosome 3), each encoding poison and antidote proteins with >200 shared amino acids, where even 2-amino-acid mismatches can disrupt antidote function.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C17 establish foundational knowledge about meiotic drivers and the wtf system, all supported by appropriate citations to prior work. These are well-established facts from the literature that provide necessary context. While not novel findings of this study, they are accurately represented.

results.result: S. pombe biology and prior observations: S. pombe exists as haploids that mate under starvation to form diploids that undergo meiosis. Isolates share >99% sequence identity with three chromosomes, yet outcrossing often yields low fertility. Disomy of chromosome 3 is the only tolerable aneuploidy and is unstable during vegetative growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C31 summarize established S. pombe biology and prior observations, all supported by appropriate citations. These provide essential background for interpreting the current findings. The information is accurately represented from the cited literature.

results.result: Experimental strain description: The Sp/Sk mosaic diploid used in experiments is heterozygous for eight wtf drivers, homozygous for Sk chromosomes 1 and 2, and heterozygous for most of chromosome 3.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 describe the experimental strain design with appropriate citations and figure references (Figure 3A). This is methodological information necessary for interpreting results but not itself a scientific finding.

results.result: Evolutionary context: S. pombe isolates carry 4-14 wtf genes that are rapidly evolving. Outcrossing generates extensive wtf heterozygosity leading to haploid spore death because Wtfantidotes are sequence-specific and haploid spores unlikely inherit all drivers. Chromosome 3 is the only chromosome tolerating disomy, and natural strains contain tandem wtf duplications consistent with unequal crossover events.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C96 synthesize established knowledge with observations from this and prior studies. The logic connecting rapid wtf evolution (C90) to extensive heterozygosity (C91) to haploid spore death (C92-C93) is sound. The observation about tandem duplications (C95) is cited appropriately. These provide important evolutionary context for interpreting the experimental findings.

results.result: Speculative evolutionary models: The authors previously speculated that wtf expansion on chromosome 3 relates to aneuploidy tolerance. An alternative model suggests frequent disomy might predate and enable wtf driver success by preventing drivers from being too costly to hosts.
results.evaluation: Claims C97 and C104 are explicitly presented as speculation (C97 cites prior speculation, C104 presents an "alternative model"). While these are interesting hypotheses consistent with the data, they lack direct experimental support and represent ideas for future investigation rather than established results. The authors appropriately acknowledge the speculative nature.

results.result: Evolutionary parallels and S. pombe mating biology: The sickle cell trait exemplifies evolutionary tradeoffs where heterozygote advantage comes with homozygote costs. S. pombe can switch mating types during clonal growth, leading to frequent inbreeding, though outcrossing can favor mutations increasing disomy.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 about sickle cell are well-established with appropriate citations and serve as an analogy. Claims C100-C102 about S. pombe mating biology are supported by citation (C100) and represent reasonable inferences (C101-C102) about population structure. These provide useful context but are not primary findings of this study.

results.result: Broader context of meiotic drive: Meiotic drive is pervasive in eukaryotes and represents a powerful evolutionary force. Examples include biased gene conversion affecting recombination protein evolution in mammals, and female meiotic drive potentially driving evolution of karyotypes, centromeres, and meiotic division timing.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C110 summarize the broader literature on meiotic drive with appropriate citations. These establish that the wtf system is part of a widespread phenomenon. The information is accurately represented from cited sources and provides important context for the significance of the work, though it represents prior knowledge rather than new findings.
